title: How Much To Save If You Want To Become a Landlord in the U.S.
description: Capital requirements for your first investment property.
content:
Real estate investing is a popular path to wealth, but the barrier to entry is cash. Unlike buying a primary home (3% down), buying an investment property typically requires 20-25% down plus substantial reserves. Banks view rental income as risky. If you under-capitalize your first deal, one vacancy or broken furnace can force you into foreclosure. This guide helps you calculate the 'Cash to Close' for a rental so you can buy safely.

Key Takeaways

  • The 25% Down Rule: Investment property mortgages usually require 20-25% down to get a decent rate. On a $300k home, that is $75,000 cash.
  • Closing Costs (4%): Investment loans have higher fees/points. Budget an extra 4% of purchase price ($12k) for closing.
  • The '6-Month Reserve': Lenders require you to show you have 6 months of mortgage payments in liquid cash after the down payment. You cannot drain your account to zero.
  • The 'Repair' Fund: You need an immediate $5,000 slush fund for Day 1 repairs (paint, locks, cleaning) before a tenant moves in.

Why It Matters (US Context)

House Hacking (living in a multi-unit property) allows you to use FHA financing (3.5% down). This is the 'Cheat Code' for aspiring landlords who don't have $100k saved.

The Investor's Bank Account

Target: $300,000 Rental Property.

1. The Purchase Cash

  • Down Payment (25%): $75,000.
  • Closing Costs (4%): $12,000.
  • Total to Close: $87,000.

2. The Safety Cash

  • Bank Reserves (6 mo PITI): ~$12,000.
  • Maintenance Fund: $5,000.
  • Total Reserves: $17,000.

Grand Total: You need $104,000 in the bank to buy a $300k rental safely.
Reality: It takes time to save this. Don't rush.

How to Save Faster

  1. House Hack First: Buy a duplex as your primary residence. Down payment drops to 3.5% ($10,500). This is how most people start.
  2. REIT Bridge: While saving, keep your money in a REIT ETF (VNQ) or HYSA. Don't risk the down payment in volatile tech stocks.
  3. Partnerships: Find a partner with cash. You provide the hustle (finding the deal, managing it), they provide the down payment. Split equity 50/50.
  4. BRRRR Strategy: Buy a fixer-upper with cash (or hard money), fix it, rent it, refinance it. This pulls your capital back out, but requires high expertise.

Frequently Asked Questions

Can I use my 401(k)?

You can take a loan ($50k), but it increases your DTI (Debt to Income) ratio, which might hurt your mortgage qualification. Ask a lender first.

Does rental income count for the loan?

Yes, banks usually count 75% of the projected rent as income, which helps you qualify. But you still need the cash down payment.

Is it passive income?

No. It is a part-time job. Dealing with tenants, toilets, and taxes takes work. If you want truly passive, buy a REIT.
